fixes.explanation: Consolation is the word. Job says, “let this be your consolation to me.” I think he's asking for the one comfort that costs his friends nothing, and that's open ears. Listening is a gift you can give without even standing up, friend.

Comfort fits the cozy picture, with safe homes and no fear. But the word in this verse is “punishment.” Job says “no rod of punishment from God is upon them.” That's the part Job says is missing from their homes.

That's true. Job is quoting what the wicked say to God: “Who is the Almighty, that we should serve Him, and what would we gain if we pray to Him?” Notice they ask what they would gain. I think that's a pretty cold way to talk to the Almighty.

A warning would come before something happens, but Job is asking about repayment. He says, “Let God repay the man himself, so he will know it.” Repay is the word, friend. Job asks that it be the man himself, and not his children.

Bitterness is it. Job says this other man “…dies in the bitterness of his soul, having never tasted prosperity.” It's a heavy picture of how a life ends. I think Job sets these two men side by side on purpose.

Strength goes with the first man, who dies “…full of vigor…” The second man's ending is different. He dies “…in the bitterness of his soul, having never tasted prosperity.” It's a heavy contrast, friend.

It doesn't work that way in Job's words. He says, “But together they lie down in the dust, and worms cover them both.” Both men end up in the same place, the one who died full of vigor and the one who never tasted prosperity. This is a heavy picture, and it isn't only about the bitter one.

False is right. Job says, “But together they lie down in the dust, and worms cover them both.” The man who dies full of vigor and the man who never tasted prosperity end up in the same place. It's a sober point, and Job makes it plainly.

Travelers are the answer. Job asks, “Have you never asked those who travel the roads? Do you not accept their reports?” He points his friends to people on the roads and asks whether they accept what those people report. The elders and priests never come up in this verse, friend.

True. Job says, “Indeed, the evil man is spared from the day of calamity, delivered from the day of wrath.” That's what he reports about the evil man. Spared and delivered are the words he uses, friend.

The text says the opposite. Job states, “Indeed, the evil man is spared from the day of calamity, delivered from the day of wrath.” Spared is the word he uses. Job isn't saying the evil man gets hit, friend.
That's the one. Job says, “He is carried to the grave, and watch is kept over his tomb.” He's carried to the grave, and a watch is kept over his tomb. It's a heavy part, so I'll let it sit.

Job paints a different picture. He says, “He is carried to the grave, and watch is kept over his tomb.” He adds that “everyone follows behind him…” Nothing in these verses says he's buried in a hurry or forgotten, friend.
